text:
I went to the garden this morning and it was a mess. It hadn't been touched in three months since grandma left. There were morning glories just all over the trellis, just this blue and it's very pretty. And then the roses that she had, that she used to cut back so precisely, they were just sprawling everywhere. And the birdbath was just completely surrounded by weeds and a robin was in there taking a bath. And I just stood at the gate with the groceries in a paper bag and my keys and I just couldn't figure out why I was coming here. Because the house is empty now. They sold it to a young couple. And they gave me until Sunday to come take what I want. But it's not in the house, it's outside. It's the smell of the dirt and the tomato leaves and the lavender that grows just in a crooked line. And she always said the lavender grows better if you don't touch it.
When I was nine, after my parents split up, she taught me how to garden. And she just knelt down next to me and she said, "You don't yank, you just ask the dirt. You ask it gently for what you need." And she was just in her sun hat, it was torn. She had a man's denim shirt on, and sunburn cream and mint just smelling her hands. And I just remember thinking, she's the oldest thing in the world. And the sweetest. Now, she's in memory care just forty minutes away. And she doesn't really recognize me. But last week I went to see her and she just looked out the window and she said, "The tomatoes need staking." And I said, "Yes, they do." "Use the twine in the shed, the brown one, not the green." And I said, "Yes, I will." And she just nodded and then she closed her eyes and I just felt she was gone. And so I came and I put the groceries on the porch and I walked in. The door was creaky. And it's just very humid and green inside. And the peonies are just collapsed over their own flowers, the flowers are brown and everything. And the little stone walkway that she built, just putting one stone on top of the other, you can barely see it because of the thyme that grows over it. And I just got down and I pulled a little weed and the dirt is just so nice and loose and just full of worms. And then Mrs. Alvarez from next door, she was working in her yard, and she said, "You're gonna get dirty." And I said, "I don't mind." And she said, "She's gonna be happy that someone is taking care of it." And she said, "She used to say the garden is a conversation. If you don't talk to it, it forgets about you." And I laughed, but I just coughed. I said, "She forgets a lot of things these days." And she said, "Not this. She asks me every time I come, 'How's the garden doing? Are the figs ripe?'" And I said, "Not yet." And she said, "When they are, you'll have to tell her." And then she went back to her yard. And I just worked for a while, I didn't even have gloves on. I just pulled all the weeds, and I got the twine and I put it on the tomatoes. And it smelled just like my grandmother's hands. And I just talked to them, "There you go. There." And by late afternoon, it looked much better. It wasn't fixed, but it just looked much better. And the sun was going down and I just sat on the bench by the birdbath and I watched the bees just stumble into the foxglove and it was just very golden and beautiful. And then my phone rang. And it was the memory care unit. And I answered and I said, "Hi." And the nurse said, "Your grandmother is asking for you. She wants to talk about the garden." So I drove there. And I got there and I said, "I'm here." And she just grabbed my hand. And her hands were very cold, but she was very strong, holding on. And she said, "The tomatoes." And I said, "Yes, I put them up. I put the brown twine." And she just smiled and she said, "Good girl." And she said, "And the figs?" And I said, "Not yet." And she said, "They'll come. You have to wait." And we just sat there and watched the sun going down. And the parking lot was just gray and nothing. And I just looked out the window and I just felt the garden. And I just squeezed her hand and she squeezed back. And then she closed her eyes and I just stayed there until the nurse came and said that she needs to go. And then I drove home. And I just stood in the garden and listened to the crickets and the garden was very quiet. But it was there.
